title: Clearing 2.45m: The High Jump's Quiet Revolution
summary: The high jump world record has stood since 1993. A new generation of jumpers is getting closer than ever. We look at the event's history and why the bar may finally be about to fall.
content:
Javier Sotomayor cleared 2.45 metres in Salamanca in 1993. Thirty-three years later, that mark still stands as the world record in the men's high jump. No athlete in the intervening decades has come within a centimetre of it. The record is not just intact — it has seemed, at various points, almost mythological: set by a Cuban athlete at the peak of his powers, in an era before some of the biomechanical analysis and conditioning science that modern athletics routinely employs.

And yet. The last five years have seen the event's ceiling approach Sotomayor's mark more closely than at any point since the 1990s. A generation of jumpers who have grown up watching video analysis of Sotomayor's technique, who train with tools the Cuban never had, are clearing 2.37, 2.38, 2.39 metres. The record is not safe.

The Fosbury Flop's Legacy

When Dick Fosbury cleared the bar going backwards at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics — a technique so unconventional that the crowd initially laughed — he did not simply win a gold medal. He rewrote the biomechanics of a sport. The Fosbury Flop, as it became known, is now the universal technique in high jump at every level. No serious high jumper uses any other method. The revolution was total and permanent.

Sotomayor's record was set using the Fosbury Flop at the extreme limits of what the technique allows. The question for modern athletes is whether refinements in the execution — in the approach run, the penultimate stride, the rotation and arch over the bar — can extract more from a technique that has been standard for nearly sixty years.

The New Generation

Gianmarco Tamberi's Olympic gold at Tokyo, Mutaz Essa Barshim's consistent proximity to the world record, and the emergence of young jumpers from multiple continents who are clearing heights that were previously rare — this is a generation that has the potential to threaten Sotomayor's mark.

The technical analysis available to athletes today is exhaustive. Every jump is captured from multiple angles, broken down frame by frame, compared against the best jumps in history. Athletes know, with a precision that was not previously possible, exactly where their technique differs from the optimal. The gap between knowing what to do and being able to do it remains significant — but the knowing is now much more precise.

The record will fall. I believe that completely. Whether it is me or someone else who does it, the record will fall. The event is moving in a direction that makes it inevitable. The only question is when.

The Women's Event

The women's high jump has its own record — 2.09 metres, set by Stefka Kostadinova in 1987 — that has proved even more durable than the men's mark. Yaroslava Mahuchikh's recent performances, including a world championship gold, have put pressure on a record that had seemed permanently out of reach. The event's standard has risen. The question of whether 2.09 is eventually bettered is as compelling as the men's question.

What It Would Mean

When a world record that has stood for more than three decades finally falls, it is an event. Athletics does not produce many moments of genuine historical significance outside the Olympic Games. A new high jump world record would be one. The sport should be paying attention — it is coming.
author: SportsKeen Editorial
